---
name: read-the-rank-clause-backwards
description: A certificate clause bounding an invariant to zero is a source of equations, not a cost; find the element the structure always contains and let the clause kill it
metadata:
  type: project
---

A colength/rank certificate reads as a *cost* — seven fields to discharge. At the degenerate
parameter one of them runs the other way and becomes a **generator of equations**. AJCR's
`DivisorAdaptation.IsCertified 0` asks `rankAtStalk Glued = 0` with `Glued` finite projective;
via `Module.rankAtStalk_eq_zero_iff_subsingleton` that makes `Glued` a *subsingleton*, and the
constant family `1` always lies in `Glued` (both equalizer arrows are algebra maps). So
`1 = 0` in every `colength j`, hence `Ideal.span {eqn j} = ⊤`, hence **every chart equation is
a unit** — and a system with unit equations is `DivEq` to the trivial one. That closed
general-`R` degree-0 uniqueness, which the landed field proof needed `Field K` *plus four
`relCurve C K` geometry instances* to get.

**Why:** the tree had been reading that clause only as something to satisfy. Nobody asked what
it *implies* once satisfied. The recipe is mechanical: find an element the carrier contains
unconditionally, then let the vanishing clause annihilate it. It also explains why the
degenerate parameter is principled rather than small — `rankAtStalk_glued` is the one field of
seven that fails at `n > 0`.

**How to apply:** when a hypothesis says an invariant of a structure is zero/trivial, ask
(a) what does that structure *always* contain, and (b) what equation does its vanishing force
on the data? Then check whether the pre-existing proof of the same conclusion took a longer
route through geometry it did not need — the diff in binders is the real result, and it is
bigger than "the field is dropped": compare full signatures, because instance binders on a
*derived* object are what a general-test consumer cannot supply at all.

Related: [[degenerate-value-can-be-principled]], [[substitute-trivial-value-in-layer-one]],
[[field-binder-may-never-have-been-used]], [[delete-the-geometry-and-retypecheck]].

description: An overclaim aimed AGAINST your own result passes every review because it looks like self-criticism; state the negative fact at exactly the strength its cited theorem has

I landed a `rep` producer at degree 0 and wrote, in two docstrings and two commit messages,
that "coverage is provably impossible at `n = 0`". **Not a theorem.** The cited result
(`not_mem_chartLocus_of_two_le_genus_zero_param`) concludes `t ∉ chartLocus`; the assembly's
hypothesis `PointwiseCoverage` quantifies over an *arbitrary* open `W ∋ t` and never mentions
`chartLocus`. The file defining both says outright that the two carriers do not meet and that
**no declaration relates them**. Only the `chartLocus`-mediated *route* is dead. I also
silently dropped the cited theorem's own `hlam`/`hχ` hypotheses when paraphrasing it.

**Why:** the error ran *against* my own result, so it read as scrupulous self-criticism and
nothing in me or a reviewer wanted to check it. That is the whole mechanism — the caveat
section is the least-audited prose precisely because overclaiming there costs the author.
And the cost is real and asymmetric: a false "provably impossible" tells the next lane not to
attempt a route that is **not** refuted, which is worse than a missing note.

**How to apply:** when writing what your own result cannot do, apply the same discipline as
to a positive claim. Read the cited theorem's *conclusion* and compare it to the *hypothesis
of the consumer* you say is blocked — if the implication between them is not itself landed,
say "the X-mediated route is dead", not "X is impossible". Carry the cited theorem's binders.
An empty locus refutes an intended instantiation, never the general statement.
